title: Daily life on horseback
hook: cooking, praying and reading the Granth in camps

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Budha Dal today: Nihang Sikhs who say the elders' army never broke camp. Your line was the old army lives. What old way did you notice someone keeping? Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

Before dawn in a riders' camp. Horses stamping in the cold. Somebody blowing on last night's coals. Nobody knows yet whether today means a long ride, a fight, or a day of hiding in tall grass. And before any of that is decided, voices start up, low, here and there among the tents and blankets: the morning prayers, said from memory. History books of this century fill up with battles and sieges. Today is about the hours in between. Today: daily life on horseback.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN IN A RIDERS' CAMP.` → `NOBODY KNOWS WHAT THE DAY HOLDS.` → `THE MORNING PRAYERS, FROM MEMORY.`

segments.voice: Start with the prayers, because tradition puts them first. Guru Ram Das left a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib about what a Sikh's day looks like. Here in paraphrase: one who calls themselves a Sikh of the Guru rises early, bathes, and remembers the Name, and keeps remembering it sitting and standing through the day. Notice what that hymn needs. No building. No fixed address. Water and a voice. The riders could carry it anywhere, and tradition says they knew the daily prayers by heart. The second thing is the Granth itself. Tradition says the bands carried copies of the scripture with them, wrapped, and kept with care, and that when the camp stopped, a place was made for it and it was opened and read, the way it is in a gurdwara. A gurdwara, in a sense, could be pitched like a tent. The third thing is the food. Riders cooked what they could get: coarse bread, roasted grain, whatever a village shared. Tradition says even here the cooking was done together, and eaten together, sitting on the ground. Put the three side by side and a picture comes out. The hunted years didn't stop Sikh practice. They made it portable. The prayers lived in memory, the scripture in a bundle, the shared meal around whatever fire there was. And when the camp moved, all of it moved with it. Prayer on the move.
screen: `RISE EARLY, REMEMBER THE NAME.` · `THE PRAYERS CARRIED BY HEART.` · `THE GRANTH OPENED WHEREVER THEY STOPPED.` · `COOKED TOGETHER, EATEN ON THE GROUND.` · then, large: `PRAYER ON THE MOVE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes somewhere new. If you can, move. Stand up and go to a different spot: the step outside the door, a different chair, the floor by a window, even the car before you start it. If you can't move, turn to face a different wall. Settle there, and breathe. Notice how the place is different and how the practice is the same. Whatever you usually do, a breath, a line of prayer, silence, do it here. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Granth, the scripture the hunted riders carried wrapped and opened wherever the camp stopped. In the riders' camps, prayers said from memory, and food cooked and eaten together. Today's word.
Your line: prayer on the move. Today, take your practice somewhere it's never been: a bus, a walk, a waiting room. See if it travels. Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs say their daily prayers, the nitnem, morning, evening and night, often from memory or a small prayer book, wherever they are; at home, travel or work, the practice goes with them.

fork.setup: you're in a riders' camp before dawn. word might come any minute to break camp and ride hard. the morning prayers take time. what do you do?
options: skip them today and make them up when it's safe.
say them now, from memory, before anything else.
wait until you reach a gurdwara.
fork.reveal: tradition says the riders kept the prayers first, from memory, wherever they were. Guru Ram Das's hymn asks a Sikh to rise early and remember the Name.

original.note: Gurmukhi for nitnem, the daily round of Sikh prayers.

trapdoor: what you thought: in a war, religion waits until peace comes.
what it means: the riders made their practice portable: prayers by heart, the Granth in a bundle, a shared meal at any fire.
what a scholar hears: Sikh daily practice asks for no fixed building, and the camps show it carried whole: the nitnem, the reading of the Granth, and the shared kitchen all moved with the riders.

That the bands carried copies of the scripture and opened it in camp, and knew the daily prayers by heart, follows common tellings; confirm.
Camp food (coarse bread, roasted grain, food shared by villages) and cooking and eating together: confirm.
